Part I

Why doctrine, and why the early Church

Every church today claims to hold the faith of the apostles. This site traces that claim back: from what the early Fathers taught, through the councils and divisions, to what the Catholic, Orthodox, Oriental Orthodox and Protestant churches teach now. It argues a case, openly: that the Oriental Orthodox churches, the Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Indian Orthodox, have kept that faith without addition or loss. That is the Oriental Orthodox conviction, and this site sets out the evidence for it. It also holds that the Eastern Orthodox are their brothers, who confess the same Christ in the language of later councils. Each church’s view is given in its own words and sources, so readers can check the case for themselves.

What doctrine is

Doctrine means “teaching,” from the Latin doctrina, translating the Greek didaskalia. It is what a church holds to be true about God, Christ, salvation, the Church and the sacraments. The New Testament already treats it as something to guard and pass on.

Why it matters

  • It is about who God is. The Arian controversy was not about words: if the Son is a creature, Christians worship a creature, and a creature cannot join us to God.
  • It is about how we are saved. The Fathers argued from salvation back to doctrine. Gregory Nazianzen’s rule, that what Christ did not take on he did not heal, decided the debates over Christ’s human mind and will.
  • It shapes worship and life. Whether the Eucharist is Christ’s body, whether infants are baptised, whether the saints are asked to pray: each of these follows from a doctrine and changes what a Christian does every Sunday.
  • It is what unites and divides the churches. Every split traced on this site, from Ephesus and Chalcedon to 1054 and the Reformation, was over doctrine. So is every reunion agreement since.

The case for the Oriental Orthodox

1

The faith of Ephesus, unchanged

They hold the first three councils and Cyril’s teaching as Ephesus received it in 431: one incarnate nature of God the Word, from two natures, with the twelve anathemas that Ephesus placed in its acts. The Antiochenes fought those anathemas until the Reunion of 433; the Oriental Orthodox never let them go. The case against Chalcedon

2

Cyril’s own words

Cyril’s own formula, “one incarnate nature of God the Word,” is still their confession, word for word. The Eastern Orthodox also honour Cyril, reading him through Chalcedon, and in 553 came back to his own phrases, “from two natures” and “one nature made flesh.” How faithful to Cyril?

3

Ancient worship kept

The liturgies of St Basil, St Gregory and St Cyril in Coptic, St James in Syriac, the long fasts, the hours of prayer and the oldest Christian kingdom in Armenia. Their practice is the early Church’s, still in use. Disputed practices

4

Confessors and martyrs

Exiled and persecuted by the empire after 451, then living under Persian, Arab and Ottoman rule, through the Armenian Genocide and the Sayfo of 1915 to the Coptic martyrs of Libya in 2015, they have kept the faith at great cost.

5

Brothers with the Eastern Orthodox

The joint commission of 1989 and 1990 found that both families hold the same faith in Christ, and proposed lifting the anathemas, including those against Dioscorus and Severus. The case here is for the Oriental Orthodox, not against the Eastern Orthodox.

Why the early Church matters

1

Closest to the apostles

Clement of Rome knew Peter and Paul; Polycarp was taught by John; Irenaeus heard Polycarp. Their witness is the nearest we have to how the apostles’ own churches understood them.

2

They received the Bible

The New Testament books were written by the apostolic generation, but it was the early Church that sorted them from other writings. Athanasius gave the first list of exactly 27 books in 367.

3

They wrote the shared creeds

The Nicene Creed and the definitions of Ephesus and Chalcedon came from their councils. Nearly every church today, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant, still confesses the Trinity in their words.

4

They met the questions first

Gnosticism, Arianism, Nestorianism and the others forced the Church to say exactly what it believed. Most later debates replay one of theirs, often with their texts on both sides.

Irenaeus of Lyons, c. 180Against the Gnostics, who claimed secret teaching, he pointed to the public teaching handed down in the apostles’ churches.
Vincent of Lérins, 434The classic test for telling true tradition from novelty: what the whole Church has held, in every age.

How each tradition uses the Fathers

Catholic

The Fathers are witnesses to Tradition, which together with Scripture is one deposit of faith, interpreted by the bishops in communion with the Pope. Doctrine can develop, as the seed grows into a tree, but not change its meaning.

Eastern and Oriental Orthodox

The Fathers are the living voice of Holy Tradition. Their consensus is the way the Church reads Scripture, and to be Orthodox is to “follow the holy Fathers.” The Oriental Orthodox accept the councils up to Ephesus (431) and read the Fathers through Cyril, Dioscorus and Severus.

Protestant

The Fathers are valued teachers but not a final authority: Scripture alone is. The Reformers quoted Augustine constantly and kept the early creeds, but held that the Fathers could err and must be tested by the Bible.

How this site makes its case

This site is written from the Oriental Orthodox side, and says so. But a case is only as strong as its evidence, so it shows what each Father actually wrote, links the full text, and marks where the evidence is divided. The Fathers did not always agree with one another: Tertullian joined the Montanists, Origen’s speculations were condemned, and Augustine and the East differ on grace. The Eastern Orthodox, Catholic and Protestant positions are set out in their own words beside the Oriental Orthodox one, so readers can weigh them for themselves. Where a judgement is needed, as in the Protestant scorecard, the method is shown and can be changed.

Part II

Who is Christ, and why the Cross?

Every question on this site comes back to the one Christ asked his disciples: “Who do you say that I am?” And the answer leads straight to the Cross, because who he is decides what his death achieved. Here is the answer of the early Church, as the Oriental Orthodox have kept it.

Part V

The road to Chalcedon

From Arius in 318 to the Council of Chalcedon in 451, the Church argued over who Christ is. Each person below pushed the question one step further. The chart places them roughly between two poles: stressing the distinction of God and man in Christ, as the school of Antioch did, or stressing their unity, as Alexandria did.

The words they argued over

Much of the dispute after 451 turned on four Greek words that the two sides used differently. Fr. Tadros Malaty’s study of the terms argues that each side heard heresy in the other’s vocabulary rather than in its faith.

Why the Oriental Orthodox reject Chalcedon

The Oriental Orthodox churches have rejected Chalcedon since 451. Their case is set out below from works by their own theologians, beside the answer the Eastern Orthodox and Catholics give, and then the Oriental Orthodox response to that answer. Both sides condemn Nestorius and Eutyches.

The Oriental Orthodox case

  • Ephesus set the standard. The Council of 431 accepted Cyril’s Third Letter with its twelve anathemas. Even its opponents said so: the Eastern bishops complained of it, and Ibas’s letter of 433 says the Chapters were confirmed. Chalcedon set them aside and put Leo’s Tome in their place. (V. C. Samuel, ch. 15; “Arguments Against OO Refuted, Part 1”)
  • “In two natures” divides. Cyril taught one Christ “from two,” with the natures distinguished “only in thought,” like soul and body in one man. A union of two natures yields one composite nature, both created and uncreated in its parts; to count two after the union is the Antiochene error. (Cyril, Second Letter to Succensus; Gregory, Letter 101)
  • Chalcedon restored Cyril’s enemies. It reinstated Theodoret and Ibas. Ibas’s letter, which calls Cyril an Apollinarian and praises Theodore of Mopsuestia, was read out and pronounced orthodox by Leo’s legate. (“The Implicit Nestorianism of Chalcedon”)
  • Nestorius approved. In exile Nestorius welcomed Leo and Flavian as teaching what he taught.
  • Dioscorus was not condemned for heresy. Anatolius of Constantinople said so at the council itself. Dioscorus had already rejected Eutyches’ errors at the first session, and later anathematized him. (Ishak, Part Four III.C; Price’s commentary on the Acts)
  • Politics drove the council. Leo pressed his Tome as part of Rome’s Petrine claims, and the court wanted to raise Constantinople over Alexandria, which Canon 28 then did. Imperial persecution followed. (V. C. Samuel, ch. 15)
  • The formula is Athanasian. Fr. Tadros Malaty argues that “one incarnate nature” came from Athanasius, and that Apollinarius borrowed and twisted it, not the reverse.

How the Eastern Orthodox and Catholics answer

  • Chalcedon built on Cyril. It received Cyril’s Second Letter to Nestorius and his Letter to John of Antioch as standards, and the bishops would not approve Leo’s Tome until it had been checked against Cyril.
  • “In two natures” does not mean two persons. The definition confesses “one person and one hypostasis,” the natures “without division, without separation.” Cyril himself signed the Reunion of 433, which speaks of “a union of two natures.” The phrase was needed against Eutyches, who denied that Christ is of one essence with us.
  • Theodoret and Ibas were restored only after anathematizing Nestorius before the whole council, and their writings against Cyril were condemned in 553.
  • Nestorius misread Leo. Leo himself condemned Nestorius; one heretic’s approval does not make a text heretical.
  • Dioscorus’s offence was real. At Ephesus in 449 he restored Eutyches, deposed Flavian, who died soon after, and refused to read Leo’s letter. Whatever his own belief, his council endorsed a man condemned for heresy.
  • The Chalcedonian Church received Cyril’s full language. The Council of 553 accepted “from two natures” and “one nature made flesh” rightly understood, and condemned the Three Chapters.
  • The formula is Apollinarian. Most historians trace “one incarnate nature” to a letter of Apollinarius circulated under Athanasius’s name.

The Oriental Orthodox response

  • On “built on Cyril”: Chalcedon used Cyril’s gentler letters but left out the Third Letter and the twelve anathemas that Ephesus had confirmed, and it struck “from two natures,” Cyril’s own phrase, from its draft.
  • On “not two persons”: the Oriental Orthodox accept that the Eastern Orthodox do not mean two persons, as the joint commission confirmed. Their objection is to a formula that Nestorius himself could welcome and that, read alone, does not exclude him.
  • On Theodoret and Ibas: the bishops shouted Theodoret down until he anathematized Nestorius, and accepted Ibas on the strength of a letter attacking Cyril. That the Council of 553 had to condemn those writings a century later concedes the point.
  • On Dioscorus: Eutyches was restored in 449 after confessing an orthodox faith, and Dioscorus condemned his errors when they became plain. Anatolius admitted at Chalcedon that Dioscorus was not deposed for his faith.
  • On the Council of 553: by accepting Cyril’s formulas, the Chalcedonian side came to the Christology the Oriental Orthodox had never left. As Fr. V. C. Samuel put it, defending Chalcedon gained nothing for orthodoxy that its critics had not held all along.

Drawn from Fr. V. C. Samuel, ch. 15, and Fr. Shenouda M. Ishak, Part Four.

Reading the evidence

The acts of the councils bear out the Oriental Orthodox account of what happened at Chalcedon: Cyril’s anathemas set aside, his phrase struck, his critics restored, and his successor deposed without a judgement on his faith. They also show that the Eastern Orthodox meant to confess Cyril’s Christ, and in 553 took back his language. Fr. V. C. Samuel, an Indian Orthodox historian who also disagreed with his own church’s official account on some points, concluded after a lifetime on the sources that the two sides held the same faith in Christ, and that what divided them was suspicion of each other’s words. He named one real difference of emphasis: the Chalcedonian teaching that Christ’s humanity has no hypostasis of its own, against the Oriental Orthodox view that it is a real, individual humanity made the Word’s own. The official joint commission reached a similar verdict in 1989 and 1990, though communion has not been restored.

Drawn from Fr. V. C. Samuel, The Council of Chalcedon Re-Examined (Oriental Orthodox Library, 2005); Fr. Shenouda M. Ishak, Christology and the Council of Chalcedon (Outskirts Press, 2013); Fr. Tadros Y. Malaty, The Terms Physis and Hypostasis in the Early Church; “The Implicit Nestorianism of Chalcedon and the Chalcedonian Fathers”; and “Best Arguments Against OO Refuted, Part 1.” The Chalcedonian reply summarises the standard Eastern Orthodox and Catholic position.

    Part XIV

    The Catholic Church

    The largest Christian communion, with about 1.4 billion members: the Latin Church of the West together with 23 Eastern Catholic churches, all in communion with the Bishop of Rome. Its head since May 2025 is Pope Leo XIV. It shares the Oriental Orthodox faith in the sacraments, the saints and the Theotokos, and the two signed a common declaration on Christ in 1973; it differs over the authority of Rome and the doctrines the West defined after the divisions.

    What makes Catholicism distinct

    Authority

    • The Pope, as successor of Peter, has full and immediate jurisdiction over the whole Church, and speaks infallibly when he defines a doctrine of faith or morals ex cathedra (First Vatican Council, 1870).
    • 21 ecumenical councils, from Nicaea to the Second Vatican Council (1962–1965).
    • Scripture and Tradition together, interpreted by the magisterium, the teaching office of the Pope and the bishops; doctrine can develop over time.

    Doctrine

    • The Filioque: the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.
    • Original sin as inherited guilt as well as a wounded nature, after Augustine.
    • Purgatory as a final purification, and indulgences.
    • Transubstantiation as the account of how the bread and wine become Christ’s body and blood (1215; Trent).
    • The Immaculate Conception (1854) and the Assumption of Mary (1950) as dogmas.

    Worship and life

    • In the Latin rite: the Roman Mass, unleavened bread, confirmation and first communion delayed until the age of reason, and celibate priests.
    • The Eastern Catholic churches keep their own Byzantine, Coptic, Syriac, Armenian, Ge’ez and Indian rites, often with married priests.
    • Devotions of the Western Church: the Rosary, Eucharistic adoration, the Stations of the Cross.

    In their words

    The Oriental Orthodox view

    Where they differ

    • Rome’s claim to rule the whole Church grew in the same years as Chalcedon: Leo pressed his Tome as Peter’s voice, and the Oriental Orthodox see in this the root of the division.
    • The Filioque was added to the Creed without any ecumenical council.
    • Purgatory, indulgences, the Immaculate Conception and papal infallibility were defined long after the early Church and have no basis in the Fathers before 451.
    • The Eastern Catholic churches were largely formed by drawing communities away from the Oriental and Eastern Orthodox, the method called “uniatism.” Catholic and Orthodox theologians together rejected it at Balamand in 1993.

    Where they meet

    • In 1973 Pope Paul VI and Pope Shenouda III confessed together that Christ is perfect God and perfect man, without mixture or division, setting aside the old charge of “Monophysitism.”
    • Similar declarations followed with the Syriac (1984), Malankara (1990) and Armenian (1996) churches, and a joint theological commission has met since 2003.
    • Both keep seven sacraments, the real presence, prayer for the dead, the saints and the Theotokos.
    • In 2023 Rome added the 21 Coptic martyrs of Libya to its calendar of saints.

      Part XV

      The Eastern Orthodox Church

      A communion of self-governing (autocephalous) churches sharing one faith, the seven ecumenical councils and the Byzantine liturgy. No single bishop rules it; the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople is honoured as first among equals. Estimates of its membership run from about 200 to 260 million, most of them in Russia, Ukraine, Romania, Greece, Serbia and the Caucasus.

      For the saints this church shares with the others, and those it honours alone, see Shared and divided saints.

      What makes Eastern Orthodoxy distinct

      Much of the Eastern Orthodox faith is shared with the Oriental Orthodox. What sets it apart is the councils and teachers it added after 451, and the Byzantine form of its worship; what sets it apart from Rome is its rejection of the papacy’s claims and the West’s later doctrines.

        Part XVI

        The Oriental Orthodox churches

        Six churches that accept the first three councils but not Chalcedon. They are in full communion with one another, though not with Rome or the Eastern Orthodox. They call their faith in Christ miaphysite, “one united nature,” and reject the older label “Monophysite.”

            The Reformation and the Protestant churches

            In the 16th century, reformers in the Western Church broke with Rome over authority, salvation and the sacraments. The movement divided almost at once, and the families below still carry those first differences.

              Part XVIII

              How close to the early Church? A Protestant scorecard (illustrative)

              Twenty beliefs and practices the early sources attest, roughly to the Council of Chalcedon in 451, with each Protestant family scored on its official teaching today. A full match scores 2 points, a partial match or one strand of the Fathers scores 1, and a clear departure scores 0. The markers were chosen because the early sources speak to them, not to favour any church, and several are ones on which Protestants match the early Church better than Rome does. Switch groups off, or keep only the markers where the early evidence is clear, and the totals recalculate.

              These are this site’s own illustrative ratings, not a measurement. The result depends on which markers are chosen and how they are weighed, which is why you can change them. Resemblance to early practice is evidence, not proof, of which teaching is true, and each Protestant family contains churches that would score differently.

              Why each marker is scored as it is

              Reading the evidence

              No score here settles which church is right. Protestants accept that many of these practices are early. Their argument is that Scripture outranks even early practice, and that some practices were early additions. They point to the Fathers who disagreed with each other: Tertullian on delaying baptism, Epiphanius against images, and Jerome on bishops and presbyters being one office at first. The Catholic and Orthodox reply is that the early Church was the one that recognised the canon of Scripture, and that its consensus shows how the apostles were understood.

              Three cautions. The apostolic churches would score near full marks by construction, but they also diverge on some markers: the Latin rule of priestly celibacy, the papal jurisdiction defined in 1870, and the Western Filioque are all later than this period. Scores describe official teaching. An Anglo-Catholic parish and an evangelical Anglican one, or a confessional and a liberal Lutheran synod, would score very differently. And the Baptist column covers mainstream and Independent Baptists together; Free Will Baptists differ from it on predestination only.

              Part XX

              The Holy Mysteries: the seven sacraments

              The Greek word for sacrament is mysterion, “mystery”: an act of the Church in which God gives grace through visible things, water, oil, bread and wine, the laying on of hands. The Oriental Orthodox, Eastern Orthodox and Catholic churches all count seven. The early Church spoke of the mysteries without fixing their number, which the West set at seven in the 12th century; but each of the seven rests on Scripture and on early practice, set out below.

              MysteryOriental OrthodoxEastern OrthodoxCatholicLutheranAnglicanReformed, Baptist

              “Rite” means the church keeps the practice but does not count it a sacrament. Anglicans call the five beyond baptism and the Eucharist “commonly called sacraments” (Article XXV). Baptists speak of two “ordinances” rather than sacraments.

              Each mystery below has a counterpart in the Old Testament, a “type” or shadow that Christ fulfilled. The apostles read the Old Testament this way, and the Fathers followed them.

              Part XXI

              The Orthodox way of life

              Doctrine is meant to be lived. Five threads of the life the Oriental Orthodox churches have kept since the desert fathers: the aim of the spiritual life, the meaning of suffering, the rule of prayer, the Liturgy, and the monastery. Each is set out with the Scriptures behind it and the words of the early Church.

              Part XXII

              Ancient heresies and the Protestant churches

              The Orthodox, Oriental and Eastern alike, see several Protestant teachings as old errors that the Fathers had already answered. Below, each one is set beside the ancient teacher who first held it and the Father or council that rejected it, with the Protestant reply. The Orthodox do not equate Protestants with the ancient heretics: most Protestant churches confess the Trinity and the creeds, and the Orthodox regard them as Christians who have lost part of the apostolic faith.

              Ancient heresies revived on the Protestant fringe

              Some movements that grew out of Protestantism went further and revived heresies that mainstream Protestants also reject.

              Socinians and Unitarians

              From the Polish Brethren’s Racovian Catechism (1605) to English and American Unitarianism: Christ is not eternal God. The error of Arius and of the adoptionists.

              Oneness Pentecostals

              Split from the Assemblies of God in 1916, teaching that Father, Son and Spirit are one person in three modes, and baptizing “in Jesus’ name” only. The error of Sabellius and the modalists that Hippolytus refuted.

              Jehovah’s Witnesses

              From Charles Taze Russell’s Bible Students of the 1870s: the Son is a created being, Michael the archangel, and the Spirit an impersonal force. Arianism again, built into their own translation of John 1:1.

              Reading the evidence

              Most of these parallels are real: Aerius, Helvidius, Jovinian and Vigilantius each held a view later Protestants adopted, and the Fathers rejected each one. Protestants answer that the test is Scripture, not who first said something, and that some of the Fathers’ condemnations went beyond what Scripture teaches. They also point out that Jerome, who wrote against three of these men, himself held that bishops and presbyters were at first the same office. For the Orthodox, the question is whether the faith of the undivided Church can be set aside by a later reading of the Bible; for Protestants, whether the early Church could add to the Bible. The Reformers themselves knew these parallels: Luther accused Zwingli of Nestorianism, and the Lutherans and Reformed condemned the Anabaptists for rebaptism.

              Part XXIII

              The Bible: canon, texts and translations

              Which books belong in the Bible, which ancient text an Old Testament should be translated from, and which English Bible each church reads. Every church on this page agrees that Scripture is inspired; they differ over its edges and its text.

              Part XXIV

              The Gnostic gospels and other forgeries

              From the 2nd century on, groups outside the Church wrote “gospels” in the names of apostles to carry their own teaching: a lesser creator god, a Christ who only seemed to suffer, salvation by secret knowledge. The Fathers named and rejected them. Many were lost until the discovery of a jar of Coptic books at Nag Hammadi in Upper Egypt in 1945, near the monasteries of St Pachomius; some scholars think the monks buried them after Athanasius’s Easter letter of 367 told Egypt which books to read. Modern forgers have added a few more.

              TextDateWhat it teachesWhy the Church rejected it
              Gospel of Thomas2nd c.; Greek fragments c. 200, full Coptic text at Nag Hammadi114 sayings of Jesus with no birth, cross or resurrection. Salvation comes by understanding his secret sayings; the last saying has Peter say women are not worthy of life, and Jesus promise to make Mary male.Named among the heretics’ inventions by Eusebius. No miracles, no cross, and salvation through secret sayings, a view many scholars call Gnostic, though whether Thomas is strictly Gnostic is debated. Some sayings parallel the Gospels; scholars debate whether any are independent of them.
              Gospel of Judasc. 150; Coptic copy found in the 1970s, published 2006Judas alone understands Jesus, who laughs at the other disciples and asks Judas to betray him to free his spirit from the body.Irenaeus already knew it c. 180 as the book of the Cainites, a sect that honoured Cain, Sodom and Judas.
              Gospel of PeterLate 2nd c.A passion narrative in which Christ is silent “as if he felt no pain” and a talking cross leaves the tomb.Serapion of Antioch allowed it at first, then read it and banned it c. 200 as used by the Docetists, who denied Christ’s real suffering.
              Gospel of Truthc. 150A Valentinian meditation: ignorance, not sin, is the problem, and knowledge the cure.Irenaeus called it a “comparatively recent writing” that agrees with none of the apostles’ Gospels.
              Gospel of Mary (Magdalene)2nd c.Mary passes on a secret revelation about the soul’s ascent past hostile powers; Peter doubts her.A Gnostic account of salvation, unknown to the Church’s lists.
              Gospel of Philip3rd c.Valentinian sayings on sacraments as stages of initiation, including a “bridal chamber.”Valentinian teaching; never used by any church.
              Infancy Gospel of Thomas2nd c.Stories of the boy Jesus working miracles, some of them cursing and killing other children.Not Gnostic, but fanciful and contrary to the Gospels, where Jesus’s first sign is at Cana.
              Arabic Infancy GospelFrom a Syriac original, perhaps 5th–6th c.; Arabic manuscripts, the oldest dated 1299Jesus speaks from the cradle to declare himself the Son of God; the Holy Family’s journey through Egypt, with healings by the infant’s bathwater and swaddling bands; the boy Jesus making clay animals come alive.Never Scripture in any church. A collection of legends drawn from the Protoevangelium and the Infancy Gospel of Thomas. Its stories of the cradle and the clay birds reappear in the Qur’an.
              Protoevangelium of Jamesc. 150Mary’s birth to Joachim and Anna, her childhood in the Temple, and the birth of Christ.Never Scripture. But it is not heretical, and its account of Mary’s parents and her entry into the Temple lives on in the feasts of the Orthodox churches.
              Gospel of BarnabasItalian manuscript c. 1600; Spanish copy c. 1800; probably composed in the 14th–16th c.Jesus denies he is the Son of God and even that he is the Messiah, foretells Muhammad by name, and Judas is crucified in his place.A medieval forgery, unknown before the manuscripts themselves. Its anachronisms and its contradiction of the Qur’an are set out below.
              Secret Gospel of MarkPublished 1958–1973A letter attributed to Clement of Alexandria quoting a secret, longer Mark.Only Morton Smith ever saw the manuscript, and its photographs. Many scholars now judge it a modern forgery; others still defend it.
              “Gospel of Jesus’s Wife”Announced 2012A papyrus scrap with the words “Jesus said to them, ‘My wife …’”.Exposed as a modern forgery in 2016; the scholar who announced it accepted that it was fake.
              More on the Arabic Infancy GospelLegends of the Holy Family in Egypt

              The book survives in Arabic, translated from a Syriac “History of the Virgin.” Most of it follows the Holy Family through Egypt after their flight from Herod, healing the sick and driving out demons on the way. One manuscript adds a stay at Matarea near Heliopolis, where they rest under a sycamore and a spring rises. The Coptic Church honours the Holy Family’s flight into Egypt with its own feast and pilgrimage sites, though from its own tradition rather than this book.

              Its opening claims to come from a book of the high priest Caiaphas, and says that Jesus spoke in the cradle, declaring himself the Son of God. The Qur’an tells of Jesus speaking from the cradle (19:29–33) and breathing life into birds of clay (3:49; 5:110), stories found earlier only in these apocryphal infancy gospels. Scholars take this as a sign of how such Christian legends circulated in 7th-century Arabia.

              e-Clavis: Christian Apocrypha, “Arabic Infancy Gospel”

              More on the Gospel of BarnabasWhy it cannot be ancient
              • No ancient witness. It survives in one Italian manuscript of about 1600 and a Spanish copy of about 1800. No Father, council or early list knows it. The 6th-century Gelasian Decree names a “Gospel of Barnabas” among rejected books, but nothing connects that lost text with this one.
              • Medieval Europe on every page. It speaks of a jubilee every hundred years, which the popes set in 1300 and shortened in 1343; of wine kept in wooden casks; and of an annual forty-day fast. Its Old Testament quotations follow the Latin Vulgate, made by Jerome over three centuries after Christ.
              • It contradicts the Qur’an. It has Jesus say, “I am not the Messiah,” giving that title to Muhammad instead, while the Qur’an itself calls Jesus the Messiah (al-Masih). For this reason many Muslim scholars also reject it.
              • Its purpose. Its account of Judas crucified in Jesus’s place matches Qur’an 4:157–158. Most scholars think it was written by a convert to Islam, perhaps a Morisco in Spain, to bring the Gospel story into line with Islamic teaching.

              Catholic Answers, “Why the Gospel of Barnabas Is a Medieval Fake,” drawing on Jan Joosten’s studies

              The Fathers on the false gospels
              Irenaeus, c. 180Four Gospels, no more and no fewer.
              Irenaeus, on the Gospel of JudasHe knew the book a century or more before the surviving Coptic copy was made.
              Irenaeus, on the Valentinians
              Serapion of Antioch, c. 200On the Gospel of Peter, after reading it himself.
              Reading the evidence

              The four Gospels were already received across the Church by the time Irenaeus wrote, about 180, and every surviving list of Scripture from Athanasius onward has the same four. The Gnostic gospels are later, written in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, mostly teach a different God and a different salvation, and were known to the Fathers precisely as the writings of the sects they opposed. Modern scholars value them for what they show about early Christian diversity, and some argue the Gospel of Thomas preserves a few early sayings. But none has a claim to apostolic origin, and their rediscovery confirmed, rather than overturned, the Fathers’ account of what they contained.
